title: The black hole photo wasn't taken, it was computed by four teams that couldn't talk to each other
dek: The 2019 image of M87's black hole came from four imaging teams working in isolation and partly deceiving one another, using Frosty the Snowman as a test image, all to prove they hadn't computed what they wanted to see into the data.
why: The first stretch is academic-career reminiscence with low information density; from minute 18 it moves into the mechanistic details of the M87 imaging and is worth hearing.
who: Engineers and researchers interested in how scientific knowledge is "made" and "verified," especially those working on large-scale distributed collaboration, data pipelines, or machine-learning interpretability.
skip: The opening 0:00–11:00, the academic-career and HPS-discipline-history reminiscence, can be skipped.

points.h: To understand how knowledge travels, first look at how it is blocked
points.body: Galison says he studies secrecy not for its own sake but as proof by contradiction: to understand a car you need to know that racing stripes and tire color don't affect function, but pull the spark plug and the car won't move. He gives the example of Freud — Freud's theory of unconscious repression and censorship came directly from the physical censorship techniques of World War I Vienna: Russian censors blotted out passages with a thick black ink they called caviar, while the Germans reset the type so you couldn't tell where something had been cut. These concrete blocking techniques echoed into Freud's theory of how the mind represses traumatic experience.

points.h: The moment of seeing the image was a double panic
points.body: The team saw the image nearly a year before the official release, and alongside the excitement came two kinds of panic. One was the fear of a leak and instantly losing control; the other was more fundamental — the history of science is full of retracted claims. He mentions a local episode that seemed to confirm inflation and later had to be retracted, and the dozens of "gravitational wave detections" in the 1960s and 70s that were all retracted, until LIGO actually measured them in 2015. Galison's doctoral thesis was titled How Experiments End, on exactly how people distinguish artifacts from real effects, so the whole following year was spent asking: what if it's this? What if it's that?

points.h: Four teams were isolated, and partly deceived one another
points.body: Inside the imaging group there were four teams, forbidden to talk to each other while working, each covering its windows, and even slightly deceiving one another about what they were doing. The procedure: each team was first given a batch of practice images, without being told what they were, and asked to faithfully reproduce each one using its best method. Some of these images were grabbed at random from the internet, some were astronomical images, some were black hole simulations, and one was Frosty the Snowman — because no one could possibly have anticipated it. Only once all four teams could accurately reproduce a test image whose contents they didn't know were they given the real data; the four teams then produced very similar results, and that was the first time they genuinely hoped the image was reliable.

points.h: Collaboration with no center is what constitutes the experiment
points.body: The camera itself is a composite: eight telescopes at six sites, which only combined can synthesize a telescope the size of the Earth and achieve enough resolution. Galison stresses this is not "many people doing the same thing" — not a crowd counting fish in a river and adding up the totals, but different people in different places doing very different things, where the coordinating activity itself constitutes the experiment. He contrasts CERN: CERN has an office you can walk into to see the director-general, whereas the EHT has a director, but the funding is dispersed, the telescopes are dispersed, the work is dispersed, and no one would agree that this experiment has a single center.

points.h: Two imaging methods, each with its own narcissism risk
points.body: The four teams used two classes of technique. Two teams used clean, the old method beloved of astronomers: treat the image as a collection of point sources and restore blurred bright patches into point-like stars, with the advantage that you can see things that were previously invisible. The other two used more modern Bayesian or forward methods: presuppose that the object has edges, is convex, is roughly somewhere in the frame, and build a cost function from deviations in the parameters, with the advantage that you can extract signal from noise that would otherwise be lost — this is how phone cameras work. The danger is that with too many assumptions you get what you are looking for, like Narcissus gazing at the spring and seeing his own reflection. So their greatest fear was exactly this: knowing what you want to see, and therefore actually seeing it.

points.h: Let the computer find the parameters itself, then try them on real data
points.body: To rule out the four teams sharing one set of expected biases, they added another layer: let the computer search the test images on its own for the parameter set that best reproduces them, then apply the settings it found to the real data. Galison says this is closer to machine learning than to AI in today's sense — not many layers, traceability not entirely out of control, quite simple by today's standards. He describes that year as "living dangerously," constantly devising new ways to challenge the image.

In Objectivity, Daston and Galison distinguish three eras in the function of scientific images: idealization from the eighteenth century onward (you want to see the ideal skeleton, not my skeleton or yours), mechanical objectivity (erase the self as far as possible and let nature write itself onto the page), and expert judgment (not the apperception of genius but trainable judgment, such as distinguishing different kinds of epileptic seizure from an electromyogram). Black hole imaging walked these three steps backwards: first the four teams each used expert judgment, then the computer mechanically searched parameters, and finally the averaged image returned to idealization.

points.h: The averaged image was a compromise argued into existence
points.body: There was a big fight inside the collaboration over whether to release the averaged image. Supporters said that way no team could claim "this is our image," but Galison finds that reason too saccharine and epistemologically unconvincing; the stronger reason is that if the individual images agree (and they did all show a bright crescent on the south side), it will show up in the average, and the average can be compared against each individual image. He gives a counterexample: if King Kong smashed a hole in the Empire State Building that was exactly congruent with the building, averaging the two would give a flat field, resembling neither tower nor hole. Opponents said the averaged image doesn't correspond to any data that actually exists. In the end they decided to average — conservative, emphasizing commonalities, downplaying individual character — and the image was released on April 10, 2019.

points.h: The value of an image is that it can surprise you
points.body: Galison says that if you want to find a rare effect, you usually design an instrument to pick it out of the noise — but then you are designing to look for a particular thing. Images work the other way round: nature can use an image to show us something we didn't anticipate. That is the ultimate surprise of image-making — you can find something that isn't on the menu of outcomes you expected. It is also why they handed out Frosty the Snowman: to make sure that even such an unexpected fictional character could show up.

quotes.text: Well, for me to understand something like how knowledge is transmitted, I want to know how it's blocked. And if I understand how it's blocked, then I understand better how knowledge works.
And then with with black holes, they're the ultimate invisible object. They're the objects that reflect no light. They emit no light. They seem impossible, right?
One of them was a Frosty the Snowman because we figured nobody could have anticipated that.
It's not just a lot of people doing the same thing. It's the coordinative activity itself that constituted the experiment.
The danger is if you assume too much you get what you are looking for and you end up like narcissists looking at the spring and seeing his own reflection.
Images are the other way around. They're nature can show us things that we had not anticipated. And I think that is the ultimate surprise that image making holds for us.
So sometimes things that seem not even real become real, fundamental and practical.
